Watch: The Reform UK leader says he "frankly wasn’t even listening" during a conversation about foreign money being donated to his party

Published 5 September 2026

Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.

His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.

Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.

In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.

In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News , Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.

Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.

The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.

When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening."

"I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film.

Undercover reporters posing as party donors met with Nigel Farage and his former chief of staff Dan Jukes (left)

"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.

"Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."

The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate.

Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.

Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.

But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics.

"They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said.

He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy".

Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.

Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations.

He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."

Speaking after watching the interview, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: "For a political party that don't like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash.

"We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them."

He added: "I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they're really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going."

Analysis: Farage may have to pay more attention

Laura Kuenssberg has been speaking to senior Reform figures and members at the party's annual conference in Birmingham

There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation

Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal .

The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.

Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China , South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.

Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.

Experts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.

The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment. Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.

Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.

At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Watch: Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport

Published 7 September 2026, 01:39 BST

Officials are investigating what caused an Amazon cargo plane to overshoot the runway after landing at Miami International Airport in a deadly incident on Sunday.

Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the plane, which was operated by 21 Air, crashed just before 14:00 (18:00 GMT).

The plane, a Boeing 767-300, crossed a road beyond the runway and hit several vehicles on the ground. It is not yet clear whether those who died were in the aircraft, on the ground, or both.

Members of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency investigating the incident, are at the site and will brief reporters on Monday afternoon.

21 Air, a charter company based in North Carolina, said it was "devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft in Miami".

Both 21 Air and Amazon said they were co-operating with the investigation.

"At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured," Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference on Sunday evening.

She added that rescue crews arrived at the scene within "seconds" of the crash.

Three of the five people injured were in critical condition, Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said.

Several of the injured were trapped inside or under vehicles on the ground, and needed to be extricated by fire and rescue crews, Jadallah added.

Over 200 firefighters responded after the plane burst into flames.

Experts who spoke to the Associated Press news agency said video footage of the plane's landing would present investigators with the question of whether or not the aircraft touched down within its designated zone on the runway - and if so, what happened.

All flights at the airport were temporarily grounded by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The incident came over Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest travel times of the year.

Locals have described the aftermath of the incident.

Grace Mercado told CBS News she was in a vehicle nearby when she saw the aftermath.

"The plane was up in smoke," she said. "It was just, it was like something from a movie. It was crazy."

Beth Tilman told the New York Times she had seen a black cloud where the plane had crashed, and had smelled an acrid stench.

"It wasn't trees burning. It wasn't mangroves burning. It was some other odour that I, honestly, had never smelled before," she said.

Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 shows that the Amazon cargo flight was travelling at 112 knots (129mph, 207km/h) as it exited the "useable runway".

In a blog post, the site said the plane came to rest near a car park that serves an Amazon warehouse and other businesses.

There were light thunderstorms and gusting winds in Miami at the time of the incident, the site says.

Kelly Nantel, Amazon's Director of Corporate Global Media Relations, said: "We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport.

"Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.

"The airplane, which was operated by 21 Air, was attempting to land when this incident occurred. We're working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will co-operate fully with any investigation."

The statement from 21 Air's CEO Keith Winters said: "Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.

"Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities, and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available."

'Incredibly difficult day' Miami-Dade mayor says after five confirmed dead

The plane had earlier departed Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The crash comes during one of the busiest travel weekends of the year in the US.

Passengers at the airport told the BBC they were frustrated by the lack of information coming from officials, with many flights cancelled or delayed as a result of the incident.

There were long queues at airline counters as people tried to reschedule travel plans, with some saying they would be forced to stay in Miami an extra night.

"The earliest I could find to fly to San Francisco was Tuesday morning," said one traveller named Faroush. "I'll probably have to find a hotel and spend more time in Miami."

The Transportation Safety Administration (TSA) said there would be 17 million travellers passing through US airports in the week leading up to Monday's Labor Day holiday.

The TSA, which screens passengers flying in the US, predicted that 2.3 million people would fly on Sunday alone.

Miami International Airport (MIA) is located near downtown Miami, and is one of the busiest airports in the country.

"Founded in 1928, MIA is America's busiest airport for international freight and second busiest for international passengers, offers more flights to Latin America and the Caribbean than any other US airport," according to its website.

About 60% of all international visitors to Florida arrive at this airport, it says.

stories.body:
Like France, the UK has always been centralised – and imposing a new political structure brings huge risks

Devolution in England is going to be messy and slow, and brings with it huge risks that Andy Burnham ignores at his peril.

The prime minister’s devolution push will be messy because Whitehall’s ingrained anxiety about handing over money and power will lead to piecemeal deals, starting with a deal for Cornwall that will lack the much-promised driving force of a newly minted mayor.

And there is every prospect that it will be slow now that the reappointed housing secretary Angela Rayner’s reorganisation of local government, creating hundreds of unitary authorities where counties and districts once ruled, is mired in judicial reviews. Some councils have run up huge debts in the last decade and it’s not clear how these debts will be divided among the new entities.

There are claims that plans to divide some existing county councils into three, four or even five unitary authorities is politically motivated and that Labour has become seduced by the prospect of retaining a presence in local government through gerrymandering.

Last week, Hertfordshire county council and Newcastle-under-Lyme borough council became the latest local authorities to send letters to Rayner , seeking clarity on how the government reached its decision in their areas.

A week earlier, Lincolnshire county council did the same. Farther south, Essex county, which is to be divided into five unitary authorities, found that the recommendation of Whitehall officials for just three new authorities was overruled by Rayner .

Supposedly, all this infighting will be resolved by Christmas and England will be ready for an entirely new map of local authorities by next May when fresh elections will be held.

Surely these councils and combined authorities, many of which are also embryonic, will struggle to become public institutions with verve, drive, knowledge and experience, able to make good decisions in time for the next election in 2029.

When devolution is the prime minister’s big idea, one that will energise Britain’s spirit of enterprise, how it works is going to be crucial. He cannot risk Reform UK and the Tories crowing about another broken promise; or how it shows the British state is clogged with officials waiting for their generous pension, and in need of a Trumpian deep clean.

Rayner’s plan is rooted in a belief that local government has failed to work properly and that structural reform is the answer, saving much more over the longer term than the estimated £2bn initial cost.

It is a belief that has no basis in academic study. It would be a relief to all of those involved in local government and devolution to know that somewhere in the world there was data illustrating how this kind of structural change improves services, saves money and, as Burnham would have it, supercharges economic growth.

Unfortunately there isn’t any such evidence. It is, to use a well-worn cliche, just re-arranging deckchairs. And it is not just because the same people will be taking up the same roles in new offices (and yes, there will need to be five head offices instead of one in Essex).

As the Institute for Government says: “Structural reforms can be necessary, and useful. But there is nothing inherently valuable about them.”

What improves services are reforms to the way public officials work, and that means difficult discussions with trade unions. There needs to be a level of accountability that is absent in significant areas of the public sector. And it will be crucial to change how public organisations relate to each other, how they work together, breaking down old silos and protective practices. It involves giving more information to local people and including them in decision making going forward.

after newsletter promotion

Geoff Mulgan, a University College London professor and the former boss of the Nesta thinktank, says devolution must answer basic questions people should know, such as how private and public services are delivered and who determines the outcome, from broadband to banking.

“Otherwise it will remain entirely legitimate for populist politicians to say that people have lost control and to claim that they are the answer,” he says.

In most countries where devolution works well, the establishment of local structures was organic, not imposed. Germany grew out of mini-kingdoms. The US started as a collection of states. The Länder in Germany, and US states, agreed to a federal government while retaining a good deal of power for themselves.

The UK is more like France. It has always been centralised, and gained in many ways from that and lost out in others. So we should not underestimate how difficult it will be to impose a new political structure on England that devolves money and power to brand new councils and mayors, or in the case of Cornwall , a cabinet committee.

The public will rightly be sceptical when so many councils under the current system have fallen for the idea that they can raise themselves up if only they borrow lots of money and “invest it” in new stuff. A new high street with hotels and leisure facilities was Woking borough council’s dream until it crashed, £2bn in debt.

To say there are huge dangers in the world of finance when local council leaders are let loose, armed with a mission to generate growth, is to understate the situation. There are catastrophic dangers waiting.

stories.title: What big issues are on the agenda as Stormont returns after summer?
stories.summary: What challenges face assembly members and ministers as Stormont returns after the summer recess?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ministers and MLAs are to return to Stormont on Monday

Published 6 September 2026

It's not even the start of a new Stormont term and already there have been leaks.

Albeit it wasn't some big scoop but a rather damp surprise for the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) MLA Colin McGrath, who took to social media saying a water leak over summer had left his assembly office looking worse for wear , external .

Even the most casual observers of politics here could guess, however, that Stormont's leaky roof problems are outweighed by the ever-slow drip of political activity inside the building - a place the assembly's freshest face will witness for himself from this week.

On Tuesday, Paul Boggs was named Sinn Féin's new West Tyrone MLA after Maoliosa McHugh - who'd already said he wouldn't run in the next election - decided to call it quits.

Boggs brings the number of MLAs who have been co-opted since the last assembly election to 14 and that figure could go up still before the upcoming election next May.

Co-options aside (that's a whole other piece), the backdrop of said looming election means parties are likely to be in fighting form when Stormont sittings resume on Monday.

No time for new minister to fix health service warns top doctor Published 20 August

'Sinn Féin will not walk away from Stormont', says Michelle O'Neill Published 30 August

Maolíosa McHugh stepping down as West Tyrone MLA Published 6 days ago

Budget deadlock

The newly-appointed Health Minister Robbie Butler will be one of those quick to feel pressure, as the 10-year anniversary of the Bengoa report - a major health reform review - approaches next month.

Pay pressures in his department and the Department of Education also make for another winter of discontent, with the prospect of strike action yet to be ruled out.

We know by now that Butler and other ministers argue that their hands are tied without a budget that can allow them to meet all their outstanding pressures.

Executive parties have been taking part in talks with Treasury officials in a bid to break the deadlock but 36 days since the legal deadline to pass a budget expired , there has so far been little sign of light at the end of this tunnel.

So much so that it prompted SDLP leader of the opposition Matthew O'Toole to issue a call to public bodies across Northern Ireland this week, asking them how the ongoing lack of financial certainty is affecting their services.

Robbie Butler signing the pledge of office at Stormont after being appointed as health minister

Whether point scoring or simply making a wider point about the consequences of not having a budget, others are also talking about the problems being stored up at Stormont.

Think tank Pivotal published a report , external last week on the issue, noting that several departments are facing massive overspends this year, including deficits of about £800m in health and £250m in education.

Money matters are a major sticking point for this executive but whether this can be resolved rests on what comes out of talks with Treasury and the secretary of state - more of those are expected to happen with the parties this week.

Other key issues

The budget, as big as it is, is only one item on the executive's to-do list before the assembly dissolves in March ahead of the election.

Already ministers have been repeatedly warned by assembly Speaker Edwin Poots that time is running out to pass remaining pieces of legislation through all their hurdles.

It's not uncommon for Stormont to sit into the small hours or hold extra days of sittings as the end of a mandate approaches - this one will be no different but there are serious question marks over some key bills.

Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald's so-called "Good Jobs" Bill which aims to massively reform employment laws has yet to get executive agreement, after the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said it had no support among business groups.

Other flagship policies including the redevelopment of Casement Park and the A5 road project also remain mothballed due to financial and legal disputes.

The reality is that as the countdown to election day gets closer the harder it will be for the executive to make decisions on major issues, for fear that any misstep could go down badly with their respective bases.

The first and deputy first ministers will be feeling the heat in their own ways

The largest parties - Sinn Féin and the DUP - will be feeling the heat in their own ways.

Sinn Féin, which became the largest party for the first time in the last election, needs to consolidate its support and show that it can deliver - without a legislative win or two in the next few months this may be hard to demonstrate on the doorsteps.

The DUP faces its own challenges of going into its first election since the conviction of former party leader Jeffrey Donaldson in June for child sex abuse offences, which he is appealing .

In July, the party moved to commission an independent review over Donaldson's actions while he was a member of the DUP, but it is not yet clear when the report will be completed or published.

Throw in fresh tensions over Drumcree , continuing rows over Irish language signage and pressure on Alliance's agriculture minister over a controversial cattle cull last month and it all makes for a battle a day.

If this current executive has anything going for it, it's that leaks of information and counter briefings against each other are much more rare than in the last executive.

Often the mood around the table is described as collegiate, even if ministers disagree on an issue.

But as one Stormont source put it recently: "You can't leak anything if there's nothing to leak. This is an executive in a holding pattern."

Sooner rather than later this executive will have to circle back to big issues that can't be ducked forever.

stories.title: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling
stories.summary: A judge ruled Next can pay warehouse workers more because it is harder to recruit and retain them.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 hours ago

Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal has overturned a key part of a landmark ruling in 2024 which found the retailer was wrong to pay its warehouse staff higher basic pay than shop floor workers for jobs of equal value.

More than 3,500 current and former employees, mainly women, had been set to share potentially more than £30m in back pay as a result of that judgement.

After Next's appeal, the law firm Leigh Day, which represents store workers, described the conclusion on basic pay as "disappointing" and said it will appeal the decision.

The tribunal accepted that Next was justified in paying higher rates because of recruitment and retention pressures for warehouse workers.

Next described the decision as a "landmark victory" succeeding on the "key issue of basic pay".

In a statement, it said: "The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for Next to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other.

"In this case, Next had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse operatives because of recruitment and retention pressures, which did not apply to the workforce in its stores. Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.

"The judgment affirms a principle at the heart of any effective employment market - that employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so."

Leigh Day said judges did uphold 2024 findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.

Next said it will now seek permission to appeal these decisions.

Both the original Employment Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal found there was no direct sex discrimination in Next's pay rates. Shop floor staff are predominantly women while warehouse workers are predominantly male.

Questions are now being asked about if this result could set a precedent across the industry. Tesco, Asda, Morrisons, and Sainbury's are all involved in similar long running claims and will be studying the findings closely.

Last year, thousands of female workers at Birmingham City Council heard how much money they will receive in a long-awaited equal pay settlement. Brighton and Hove City Council is also facing over 1,000 equal pay cases.

In an interview with the Financial Times , John Healey said the conflict in Iran would probably have a strong influence on his first budget on 28 October. Continue reading...
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chancellor says he wants to ensure country has ‘buffer’ against uncertainty as global bond yields hit 18-year high

The chancellor has indicated that the UK will face a tough budget next month due to Trump’s war in the Middle East.

In an interview with the Financial Times , John Healey said the conflict in Iran would probably have a strong influence on his first budget on 28 October.

Healey, who succeeded Rachel Reeves when Andy Burnham became prime minister in July, told the newspaper he wanted to ensure the country had a robust “buffer against uncertainty” amid increasing global instability.

However, economists have predicted that Healey will need to raise taxes or implement significant cost-cutting measures to protect the £24bn fiscal headroom that Reeves had after her March statement.

“What’s happening in the Middle East is hitting inflation , it’s hitting growth, it’s hitting borrowing costs,” Healey said. “It’s part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it’s one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other [countries].”

Healey declined to say how much headroom he aimed to have, but insisted he and Burnham were “in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules”.

The newspaper said he planned to stick to Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledges not to raise taxes on “working people”, such as income tax, national insurance contributions or VAT, and was also not expected to raise the rate of corporation tax.

The public finances are under pressure from soaring global bond yields , which hit an 18-year high earlier this week. Bond yields have a significant impact on government spending plans, as higher yields drive up borrowing costs.

Healey has faced criticism for failing to commit to the goal of raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. In June, he resigned as defence secretary because he was unable to get the Treasury to commit to the target, in what was seen as a fatal blow to Keir Starmer’s government.

Acknowledging tough economic conditions, Healey said: “The country’s under pressure. People are under pressure with the cost of living. Households are feeling that. We’re concerned about the cost of living, and we’re concerned about the cost of business.”

He also said he was committed to cutting the welfare bill. “We must cut the cost of welfare, we have to get more people back into work,” he said. “I know that some of the decisions I must take – and will take – will show the benefits in years to come.”

Jim O’Neill, the cross-bench peer and economist who advised Burnham as he prepared to enter Downing Street, has suggested that the prime minister could reassure the bond markets by taking “credible actions” to rein in the “excesses” of welfare spending and the pensions triple lock.

Speaking to Times Radio earlier this week, he said: “If you have the markets carrying on doing what they’re doing globally … eventually they’re going to have absolutely no choice [but to cut spending] because the penalty of the debt servicing cost and the knock-on effect to other markets including mortgage rates will be too severe for a government to resist.”

after newsletter promotion

The triple lock, introduced in 2010, means that state pension increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5% – whichever is highest. It has led to an increase of about £16bn in the state pension bill.

On Saturday morning, Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the government could consider an Australian-style system.

He suggested that the state pension could increase in line with workers’ earnings, with an inbuilt “temporary lock” to safeguard against a decline in average wages due to recession or high inflation.

“It’s a reasonable way to increase the state pension over the long run that’s not as expensive but still generates increases,” he said.

Reform UK has said it would cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare payments, net zero investment and overseas aid. Speaking at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham, its economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, also pledged to reduce the number of civil servants.

stories.title: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam
stories.summary: About one million people - mostly women - are owed pension tax relief and will be contacted by HMRC.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 7 September 2026, 00:16 BST

You may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how you are eligible for top-up payments - and it's not a scam.

Those entitled are low earners who have missed out on the money because of the way the pension they pay into is administered.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) will write to people over the next few months, explaining how to receive the payment. Typically they will be due £70, but that may vary considerably depending on their circumstances.

Anyone eligible - the vast majority of whom will be of working age rather than pensioners - will be contacted automatically. But, if you receive a letter, there are various checks you can do to ensure the letter is genuine so you don't get hoodwinked.

What's the letter about?

When you pay into a pension, the government allows some of the money that would otherwise have been paid in tax to go towards your pension instead. This is known as tax relief , external .

For relatively complicated reasons, some low earners whose employer used what's known as a Net Pay Arrangement pension scheme received less than those whose pension was administered through a Relief at Source scheme.

Employees have no control over the type of scheme that's used, so the government has decided to make up the difference to those who have missed out, through what's called a low earner's pension payment.

Typically, to qualify, they would have earned close to, but not more than, £12,570 a year (the starting point for paying income tax). As a result of not being taxpayers, then cannot have their tax bill reduced so they will receive a payment instead.

The single payment initially relates to the 2024-25 tax year, but automated annual payments for those in the same situation in later years could be paid subsequently.

How can I check the letter is for real?

Customers don't need to apply. If eligible, you'll be sent information by HMRC - the UK's tax authority - in a letter or through your online personal tax account , external .

HMRC will not text, email or call you about it. If you receive such a call or message, it is a scam. Also, it will never ask you to transfer money, or ask for PIN codes or passwords.

Other ways to check contact is smooth and genuine include:

Making sure HMRC has your latest address

Searching Gov.uk for "check if a letter you've received from HMRC is genuine", and look for "Low Earner's Pension Payment"

HMRC also has advice on spotting a scam , external

Customers will be asked to provide their bank details through their personal tax account. Customers who are digitally excluded will be able to phone HMRC to accept their payment instead

"We know some people may be cautious about unexpected contact, which is why we provide clear information about what to expect and how to verify the contact is genuine," said a HMRC spokesman.

"Customers can check a letter is genuine on Gov.uk and should only respond via official HMRC channels."

Is everyone expected to get paid?

If you are eligible, you will need to respond to the HMRC letter through official HMRC channels to receive the payment, taking care not to be caught out by copycat scams. HMRC holds certain data but not the bank details of those who are eligible.

Sir Steve Webb, partner at pensions consultancy LCP and a former pensions minister, said he was shocked at how few people the government expected to actually receive the payment.

The government has estimated the cost of the project to be much lower than if everyone who was eligible took up the payment.

"The process of getting these payments to the right people is going to be incredibly painful and there is a real risk of huge non take-up," he said.

"It is vital that communications are effective to make sure that people get the money to which they are entitled."

HMRC says it will run an awareness campaign using social media and other channels.

The charity Clothing Coventry provides free second-hand clothes, shoes, and school uniforms to families who are in poverty

Published 7 September 2026, 09:20 BST

Thousands of families saved money on school uniforms this summer through a charity scheme providing pre-loved and donated clothing for free.

Katie Wilson, CEO of Clothing Coventry, said parents were able to select items they needed and families saved an average of £69 by going to its uniform events that ran across three weeks.

Wilson said the average cost of a school uniform is estimated at £249.58 per child and that "remains a real challenge" for many families, and the charity has helped more than 2,700 children prepare for the new school year.

"Projects like this only happen because people give their time, resources and support - thank you to every volunteer who joined us," she added.

Katie Wilson, CEO of Clothing Coventry located in the Hillfields area

Across the events, the charity distributed 15,005 uniform items, including:

1,869 polo shirts

2,807 shirts

2,388 jumpers

183 blazers

119 ties

453 logoed PE kit items

1,531 pairs of shoes

2,787 pairs of boys' trousers

616 pinafores

1,092 skirts

900 pairs of girls' trousers

260 sixth-form outfits

Alongside donated and pre-loved uniforms, it also supplied 4,659 brand-new items to 2,142 children.

A further 60 families received £30 uniform vouchers when the charity was unable to provide a blazer for their child's school.

Wilson said blazers and logoed PE kits were among the most requested items, and despite additional purchases and generous donations, demand outstripped supply in some cases.

"We could have given out probably 600 blazers if we had them, we didn't have enough to help everyone who came.

"The hope is that we can help everyone with a little bit of something" she told BBC CWR.

'Made a huge difference'

The programme, now in its fourth year, is supported by Coventry Building Society.

"While we can never guarantee every item, in every size, for every school, we are proud to say that no family who attended our events left empty-handed," Wilson said.

One parent who used the service said getting uniforms for their children had been a major concern.

"As a family with eight children and a very limited income, getting school uniforms for all our children was a big worry for us," they said.

"The support we received made a huge difference and took away a lot of financial stress.

"It helped us make sure our children could go back to school with the uniforms they needed. We are truly grateful to everyone who made this possible."

Clothing Coventry will reopen for school uniform requests on 14 September and said families can access uniform support throughout the year, not just during the summer holidays.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Bond market volatility means John Healey will have to take tough decisions, soon, if he wants to meet spending pledges

I n John Healey’s bright Treasury office, overlooking St James’s Park, the artwork has not changed since his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, selected a row of Bridget Riley prints in her feminist rehang . Judging by the signals emerging from No 11 about the chancellor’s 28 October budget, not much else has changed either.

Voters listening to Andy Burnham’s promises to overthrow 40 years of neoliberalism and vanquish the ghost of Margaret Thatcher would be excused for expecting a radical policy reset. Early signs suggest they may be disappointed.

Healey will give a speech about growth policy on Monday in his bluff, reassuring style, less than six months on from Reeves’s Mais lecture . He is expected to lean heavily on two of her favourite themes: investment and devolution.

That’s hardly surprising. The UK economy has been held back by decades of underinvestment, and growth has been far too concentrated in London and the south-east.

But the speech seems likely to be followed up six weeks or so later with a “steady as she (or rather he) goes” budget – with key decisions, including when the UK will be spending 3% of GDP on defence, deferred.

When he resigned in June, Healey was adamant that the UK should set a “headmark date” of 2030 for hitting the 3% target. Treasury sources indicate that he has not changed his mind, yet he has made clear he intends to defer setting out a timeline until next year’s spending review.

That suggests Reeves’s promise of one major fiscal event a year – the autumn budget – with a low-key forecast in the spring has been ditched.

Usually, the budget before a spending review would set out the “envelope” – the broad path of future public spending – and, where necessary, the tax rises to finance it, leaving the details to be hammered out later. But the priorities for 28 October appear to be more immediate. Healey will fill in the gaps in the defence investment plan – the one he resigned over three months ago.

There may be also modest further moves towards giving consumers “breathing space” from higher energy bills in January – though judging by the mood music , it will not be funded, as the Trades Union Congress has urged, by a windfall tax on banks .

Healey told the Financial Times this weekend: “People look at the banks largely as big profit-making multinationals, but their fundamental role is too often overlooked. That’s something that’s strong in my mind.”

There is some logic for projecting what the chancellor has called “steadiness”. He has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, where volatility in government bond markets was a hot topic.

Higher interest rates on the Treasury’s debt pile already appear to have wiped out up to half of the £24bn headroom Reeves left against her fiscal rules.

Up to another £4bn is expected to have evaporated as a result of lower-than-forecast migration, and Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills will have to be paid for, too.

It must be tempting to paper over the cracks and hope for the best. But the truth is that it will be all but impossible to raise defence spending to 3% by 2030 and avert the Whitehall funding squeeze pencilled in by Reeves for the back end of the parliament without raising taxes.

Last year’s spending review was predicated on generous increases in spending for key departments including the NHS and defence for Labour’s first two years in power, followed by a much tougher three years.

after newsletter promotion

That means, as Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies told me, “things are so tight that if the government knows for sure, for example, that they want to increase defence spending to 3% by the end of the parliament, that would mean that to stick within the current plans, you’d have to hold all other departments, including the NHS, flat.” She added with typical understatement: “That seems pretty unlikely.”

Miller said: “If you don’t want to do that, you probably want to find the money now, for the spending review next year. If you really want to get defence to 3%, that is a real challenge … the budget is the right time to be making preparations that would allow that to be possible.”

That’s an extremely tough message to announce for a government that claims to be “bringing back hope”.

One approach would have been to point to the fragility of the global environment – Iran, Ukraine, Donald Trump’s tariffs – and ditch some of Labour’s manifesto promises on tax and spend. But Burnham has already rejected that idea.

There is no doubt more to be done on reforming welfare – so that more young people are encouraged into work instead of left without help, for example, as Alan Milburn’s forthcoming review is expected to recommend. And certainly, Burnham’s erstwhile friend Lord O’Donnell is right that the triple lock pensions promise should go.

But that is unlikely to take Healey to the £10bn-ish additional spending he needs to get to 3% of GDP – let alone the 3.5% Labour has promised by 2035 – while still convincing the bond markets there is a plan for balancing the books.

As the Resolution Foundation pointed out this week, the 3.5% target looks impossible to meet without tax rises on middle-earners – who still face less of a burden on average than in many other major economies, but may feel otherwise.

Burnham’s choice of Healey as chancellor read like an endorsement of 3% defence spending by 2030. Postponing the decision will just unleash another six months of the destabilising speculation so depressingly familiar from Reeves’s tenure in No 11. Healey should bite the bullet at the budget and take the tough decisions now.

stories.body:
Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis

T he greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population . The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy.

Nowhere has the tension between this proposition and reality become more palpable during this sweltering summer than in the conversation over air conditioning.

If the atmosphere were to warm more than 3C above the average temperature in the preindustrial era, a prospect that looks ever more likely given the lackluster efforts to reduce carbon emissions , one in six of the world’s largest cities would suffer at least one heatwave per year lasting more than a month, according to the World Resources Institute . Low-income countries would suffer, on average, 6.9 heatwaves per year. Delhi would suffer at least 140 days with temperatures hitting at least 35C (95F).

Demand for AC around the world will inevitably accelerate as the atmosphere continues to warm. Ninety percent of households in the US and Japan enjoy artificial cooling. But in Indonesia, the share is only 9%. In India, it is 5%. Of the 2.8 billion people living in the hottest parts of the world, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), only 8% currently possess AC. These countries are populous, they are generally poorer and they will get particularly hot as climate change progresses.

The global stock of air conditioners in buildings is expected to mushroom to 5.6bn by 2050, up from 2.5bn today, according to the IEA . In India alone, installed AC inventory will rise from 48m units in 2020 to 1.1bn in 2050, a 23-fold increase. Even if the world met the emissions targets laid out in the 2015 Paris climate accords – which is not going to happen – an average of 40% to 50% of the population in many of the world’s warmest countries would still require AC.

This is going to require a lot of energy . Scientists at Harvard’s School of Engineering and applied sciences estimated that in India and Indonesia, demand for power just for cooling in 2050 could be as high as 75% of their current total annual electricity demand.

This poses a challenge for the climate. In 2022, energy for cooling, mostly for residential and nonresidential space cooling but also to maintain cold chains for food and pharmaceutical production, and to cool transport, accounted for roughly 2.5bn tons of CO2 equivalent emissions, according to a United Nations report , about 7% of total emissions. In the absence of further strategies to improve energy efficiency and improve passive cooling techniques, it would rise to nearly 8bn tons by 2050.

So what does one do? Apparently, 58% of the French would rather “suffer from the heat than install an air conditioner in order to protect the environment”. But these sentiments cannot drive the world’s response to a warming world. To fight the battle against climate change requires, in fact, facilitating access to AC for billions of people who are now at risk of facing a hotter planet without the technology to protect themselves and their economies.

This proposition doesn’t rest only on arguments from ethics – although there are plenty of those. For starters, there is substantial evidence that air conditioning reduces heat’s impact on health. One study of US data found that the lethality of days hotter than 80F (27C) declined by about 75% from 1900 to 2004, almost entirely due to the adoption of residential air conditioning. Asking countries not to deploy AC is tantamount to accepting higher mortality.

Another powerful reason is that limiting access to air conditioning will set back economic growth. There is abundant evidence that excessive heat in the workplace reduces labor productivity and that air conditioning mitigates the decline . Heat can also stymie student achievement, eroding human capital.

Those living in India, Bangladesh, Indonesia or other unbearably hot places wherever will not heed the call to resist AC. Demanding unrealistic policies that are detrimental to their development is a straightforward strategy to ensure these countries do not cooperate with the effort to slow climate change. Campaigns from the west to stop hydropower in Africa, (even as westerners also called to stop developing fossil fuels on the continent) delivered little and engendered ill will. Trying to limit their access to AC would do the same.

Whether it is to power industries, improve transportation, or cool homes and workplaces, achieving faster economic growth will require poor hot countries around the world to consume more energy. Their economic development is indispensable for the global battle against climate change.

Just as fans of depopulation must understand that innovation needs people , fans of shrinking humanity’s footprint on the planet to prevent climate change misunderstand how humanity has prospered despite environmental constraints: through innovation. The path to decarbonization requires figuring out how to produce zero-carbon energy on a vast scale everywhere. It will be easier to do this in a rich world with AC and refrigeration than in a poor hot one.

stories.title: Cost of living on many minds ahead of Manx election
stories.summary: Residents, businesses and charities are focused on the economy ahead of the general election.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Growing the economy has been billed as a top priority for the majority of candidates

Published 7 September 2026, 06:46 BST

Residents, businesses, and charities say they are feeling the pinch of rising costs, with many describing the economy as a key priority ahead of the Isle of Man general election.

Several independent shops in Ramsey said custom was down and running costs had become harder to manage, while the island's foodbank said demand for support had doubled in two years.

The Isle of Man Chamber of Commerce warned the Island faced "a very hard five years" ahead, citing a shrinking tax base and the recent loss of many high‑earning jobs.

Candidates have been urged to explain how they will fund their plans, support businesses, and reduce the pressures on working families.

Residents in Douglas said rising prices were affecting everyday life, with several describing the cost of living as their biggest concern ahead of the election.

Sharon Cox, from Douglas, said life was "not affordable.. especially for older people and vulnerable people".

Prices were rising "not just by pennies", but by "25 or 30 pence" each time she visited the shops, she added.

Sharon Cox said daily life on the Isle of Man had become unaffordable

Mum-of-one Caitlin Gibson said she was living with her mum and struggled to save anything while caring for her young daughter.

She said: "I can't really afford to move out. I can't afford to save anything, so everything I earn, which is very little in the first place, is going on my baby."

Another Douglas resident, Andrew Cairns, said rising fuel and energy costs were having "a massive impact".

Andrew Cairns said he could notice prices rising month on month

"Petrol is going up, electric, gas. You've only got to go in a shop a month apart and you can see the prices rising," he added.

He said it was something on his mind ahead of election, adding there was "a lot we can do to cut down our costs".

A number of businesses described the last few years as some of the hardest they had faced.

Tania Dolores has run a shoe and accessory store in Ramsey for more than 10 years

Tania Dolores, from Tania Dolores Shoes and Accessories, said: "Every day is a struggle. We are not making what we used to make."

She said her takings were "exactly the same amount of money as ten years ago", but that her bills were "much higher".

Amy Salter, from the Brunch cafe, said the cost of supplies and energy had changed how the family business operated.

When the business opened three years ago, it was "a lot easier than it is now", she said, adding that even small price rises in stock were having a big impact.

Linda Murphy wanted candidates to be looking out for small businesses

Linda Murphy, from Oma Sustainable Living, said footfall dropped sharply after government services were removed from the Post Office earlier this year.

She said she wanted to see in charge "somebody who understands and is looking out for small businesses, somebody who understands the value of the community, the high street and what it benefits".

'Not earning enough'

Chairman of the Isle of Man Foodbank David Gawne said the third sector was also seeing the impact, and said the charity had become "something of a barometer" for the island's economic pressures.

"Two years ago, we were giving out 200 parcels a month. We're now giving out 400 parcels a month and we're pushing that boundary now," he said.

He explained that 80% of people it supported were working full time, but "not earning enough now to be able to support themselves or support their family".

Gawne said many families were living on a financial knife-edge.

"A lot of people are just one payday away from relying on the food bank… that is a reality for a lot of people."

He called for the next administration to prioritise the economy.

Claire Watterson said the next House of Keys needed to be ready for a tough five years

Business lobby group the Isle of Man Chamber of Commerce said the island was entering "a very hard five years" of economic challenges, warning that pressures on public finances and the loss of high‑earning jobs had created a difficult environment for both households and businesses.

She said that after decades of economic growth, the latest statistics released by government showed the economy had declined by 7.4% in the two years to March 2024.

And she added that in the last year, a thousand jobs had been lost in the export sector, which included financial, insurance, and manufacturing sectors.

She described the figures as "incredibly concerning", with the true impact of artificial intelligence on the workplace yet to be quantified.

Watterson called for an election focus on national issues rather than local.

"What we are voting for in September is our national government… how we are going to grow the Isle of Man economy and set us apart on an international stage," she said.

stories.summary: Recent analysis showed the construction sector needs an extra 2,200 workers a year to meet demand.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Cian Halliday, 26, became a joiner after being made redundant in recent years

Published 6 September 2026

A long-term plan and additional funding is needed to create more placements for young people within the construction industry, according to one housing association boss.

Iwan Trefor Jones, chief executive at Adra, said it was important that organisations worked together to make sure "that there are opportunities for young people".

Adra had seen a rise in demand in its academy scheme, with one of their recent openings attracting 108 applicants for only six positions.

The Welsh government said work was already under way "to boost construction skills" and new apprenticeships were set to launch later in the year.

Recent analysis by the Federation of Master Builders showed that the construction sector was facing a shortfall of labour and needed an additional 2,200 workers a year in order to meet demand.

Steven Walker, a construction manager with Williams Homes, said it was "really important" that more young people came into the construction industry.

"We have an ageing workforce across the country" he said. "It's really important that young people are being pushed through to be work ready... to be the next generation of construction workers."

There was always room for more workers, he added.

"We can always create the space for young people to come and work on our construction sites.

"We buddy them up with an experienced worker, we show them the ropes, we give them the training, we look after them, we interview them regularly to see that they're OK and that they're looked after."

Steven Walker wants to see more young people getting into construction

He mentioned schemes like Academi Adra give young people hands-on experience on the job.

"The classroom-based teaching is really important. It prepares them for the work... and then when they come to us, they'll actually put into practice what they've seen in the classroom.

Jones said that it was vital there were enough opportunities in place.

"It's really important that organisations like Adra work in partnership with other organisations to make sure there are opportunities for young people."

Iwan Trefor Jones believes that a long-term plan is needed "to support the funding of placements in work, to support young people"

Speaking at one of Adra's developments of over 58 social and affordable homes in Bangor, Jones said additional funding was needed to give more young people opportunities to get into the sector.

"There's a need for a long-term plan, but also a plan is nothing without the funding behind it," he said.

"We need some kind of assurance that there is a long-term plan to support the funding of placements in work, to support young people into employment and to support employers."

The Academi Adra scheme was established in 2021 with the aim of providing young people with skills and experience in the workplace, offering courses in construction.

Two-hundred-and-thirty participants have been supported since the launch of the scheme, with the most recent course having 108 applicants for only six positions.

Elin Williams, who oversees the work of the Academi, said funding had been needed to offer more young people the chance to join similar schemes.

She said: "We've been very lucky to be able to have some external grant funding to allow us to run some courses and pay for placement opportunities.

"We're calling for more funding for opportunities and projects like Academi Adra... We want to carry on to develop and expand to meet the rising demand that we're seeing."

Elin Williams is head of community services for Adra

In recent months, Welsh figures , external suggested the proportion of young people in Wales who are not in education, employment, or training (Neet) had risen sharply.

They increased to 17% and returned to levels last seen around 2013, according to Welsh government figures.

Cian Halliday, 26, a carpenter from Llanrug, had been made redundant during the Covid-19 pandemic, something he said had been "difficult, and a struggle".

"Academi Adra were offering courses, and almost 16 weeks of work experience and at the end they decided to keep me on as a labourer. I did that for a year," he said.

"Then they offered me an apprenticeship and I chose to be a carpenter."

He said that being made redundant had been very tough.

"It was difficult, and a struggle to find work, so I decided, the minute this opportunity came up, to start a new job."

While looking for work, Cian said there had not been enough opportunities for young people like him.

"I was happy enough to change careers. I jumped at the opportunity and never looked back," he said.

Daniella Williams says the construction industry is "a great sector to get into"

Daniella Williams, 35 also got into the construction industry after a period of not being in work following an illness.

"I used to work within the NHS. I had problems with my health and I had children, so left that job, and I really wanted to get into an office-based job," she said.

Williams followed a course with Academi Adra to get into an administrative role.

"It's changed mine and my children's lives... I've been able to save, I've bought my own car, and it's given me so much more confidence," she said.

"I've been able to achieve so much that I wasn't able to before, and it's inspired my children as well to go on and do bigger and better than myself."

Williams said she was also passionate about helping inspire young girls to follow careers in the construction industry.

"'I work with schools... especially to get girls into construction.

"It's not just bricks and building, there are all kinds of different things. We work a lot with local companies, and it's a great sector to get into, I really enjoy it."

'Significant growth'

Local colleges had also seen a rise in demand.

Aled Jones-Griffith, CEO of Grŵp Llandrillo Menai, said there had been a "significant growth" in the number of young people who had undertaken construction.

He said: "Our enrolment has increased by 28% since 2025-26 to a record 461 learners this year.

"To meet this demand, we have invested significantly in redeveloping our workshops, recruiting additional staff and buying additional course resources.

"However moving forwards, we need additional funding to maintain this high level of provision and effectively minimise Neets in our community."

'It's about health, jobs and opportunity'

With the rise in demand for homes to be built, CHC said that opportunities needed to be made to end the "housing emergency".

Clarissa Corbisiero, deputy chief executive at CHC, said: "Investing in our homes is the best investment we can make in Wales' economic health.

"In building 20,000 new social homes over the next four years, housing associations can deliver over 14,000 jobs per year during construction.

"By aligning our housing goals with a bold construction skills strategy, we can turn a national emergency into a wave of opportunity for every community.

"Ending the housing emergency is more than bricks and mortar - it's about health, jobs and opportunity."

The Welsh government said: "We are committed to developing a Welsh skills system fit for the future. Work is already under way to boost construction skills with Level 2 apprenticeships in bricklaying, site carpentry, scaffolding and building maintenance set to launch later this year.

"Construction will also be included in new VCSE qualifications from September 2027.

"A skills audit is currently under way to provide a clear, cross government view of current and future workforce needs across Wales.

"A future Skills Summit is being held this October that will bring together employers, educators, training providers and policymakers to help shape reforms to vocational skills training in Wales."

stories.title: Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation
stories.summary: Firms like Meta, Google and TikTok should face "substantial" penalties if they don't give the option, minister says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Anika Wells says social media companies should offer option to switch off algorithms

Published 7 September 2026, 04:40 BST

Australians would be able to switch off social media algorithms under draft legislation to be proposed this week.

Communications Minister Anika Wells, who last year helmed the government's world-first social media ban for under-16s, said the digital duty of care laws would ensure "some basic safety protections on an industry that hasn't had to observe it".

If tech firms such as Meta, Google and TikTok did not give the option to turn off algorithms, they should face "substantial" penalties, she said.

Some members of the opposition have criticised the proposal, with Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor saying he was "highly sceptical" and arguing the move could amount to censorship.

The government will be taking "expert advice" on whether users would have to opt in or out of the algorithms feeding them content online, Wells said.

This means that, as with its social media ban , the government is looking to bring in legislation before fully hammering out the specifics of how it would work.

"We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds," Wells told the ABC on Monday.

"We know that a lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility that they get out of it, seeing local businesses in their suburb.

"A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm. But we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place and they should respect that choice.

"Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards."

But she admitted that so far no tech firm had been fined for not enforcing the social media ban, despite research consistently showing that the vast majority of under 16s who were on platforms before the ban was introduced last December, still use them .

Some members of the opposition have said they support the idea in principle, but others argue it is an attempt to curtail freedom of speech.

Taylor told News24 he feared this was "an attempt by the government to censor social media" and that Labor should first try to plug holes in the social media ban.

Speaking to Channel Nine's Today show, Wells said: "This isn't about censorship. This is about identifying risks or making big tech identify the risks on their own platform and making big tech mitigate against those risks on their platform."

Last week, high-profile consent advocate Chanel Contos gave a speech at Australia's National Press Club calling on the government to seek an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds, making it harder for tech firms to find a way round any reforms.

She argued algorithms were fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia and exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" material.

The draft legislation is expected to be introduced in the coming days. As well as addressing algorithms, it is also expected to put an onus on platforms to stop harmful content, such as illegal pornography and videos promoting disordered eating, from being shared.

stories.title: How long could you manage on £3 of food a day?
stories.summary: It wants people to experience what it is like for people facing food insecurity.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lisa Vincent, who runs Eat Social, an organisation supporting people facing food insecurity, is challenging people to spend just £3 of food a day

Published 7 September 2026, 05:57 BST

A sandwich shop is challenging people to survive on just £3 of food a day to highlight the growing number of people facing food insecurity.

Eat Social, which operates a cafe in Wensum Street, Norwich, is launching the campaign in October, asking people to sign up to take part in the two-day task.

It comes as the latest figures from the Food Foundation show one in six families with children are facing food insecurity.

Lisa Vincent, who set up the community interest company after hearing stories of children presenting with diseases caused by malnutrition, said the situation was "unacceptable" and she wanted the challenge to raise awareness.

Lisa Vincent opened The Sandwich Shop to help raise funds to support families in need with community meals

She added: "Food insecurity is not just about hunger but also poor nutrition in diets, the anxiety of not knowing where your next meal is coming from.

"Living off £3 of food a day is going to be very boring, bland and probably not very nutritious. It is just about satiating hunger in the immediate moment."

Vincent based the challenge on research showing the lowest income families are feeding themselves on £25 a week per person, which works out at about £3 a day.

"We want to raise more awareness of this and for people to understand, this is tough," she said.

Lisa Vincent stands outside The Sandwich Shop, which opened in Wensum Street, Norwich, earlier this year

Eat Social's sandwich shop venture launched three months ago and it puts 100% of its profits towards its community meals programme , external , providing nourishing meals to groups in schools.

People taking part in the £3-a-day challenge are also being asked to donate the remaining money they would have spent on food towards this project.

More stories from Norfolk

Lidl set to beat Aldi in race for town supermarket

Century-old bridge could get £10m repair cash

New machine could be part of council pothole push

Vincent was spurred to start the project after feeling "disgusted" at stories of malnutrition affecting primary school pupils in West Earlham , Norwich, with a headteacher reporting children with bowed legs.

She said: "Poor nutrition in childhood affects brain development and physical development, and you can't get that back.

"Once that development's been hampered, you could have a brilliant diet, but you are not getting that back."

Food prices continue to rise, putting more pressure on families

Food prices remain a concern and there are fears they could rise following this summer's extreme weather , which resulted in poor crop yield, and as further climate changes are predicted.

A government spokesperson said it is determined to turn the tide on poverty, using schemes including a £1bn Crisis and Resilience Fund to help councils tackle food poverty.

"Our recent statistics show that effort is beginning to make a difference - household incomes have risen 5% in real terms, food bank usage has fallen and food insecurity is down," the spokesperson added.

"To ease cost-of-living pressures we have brought forward a wide range of measures including raising the National Minimum Wage , suspending tariffs on everyday staples, leading to lower prices at the till."

Hannah Worsley, project manager for Norwich Food Bank, said people who had already made changes to their lifestyle since the cost-of-living crisis began were still struggling to make ends meet.

She said: "Several years ago, the problem people were facing was a one-off thing, like losing a job, which was then resolved and people would be back on their feet able to cope again.

"Now, we're seeing people who've made cuts maybe eating less or not using certain facilities like their cooker or their washing machine and it's still not enough to live on."

She hopes the £3-a-day challenge will help people empathise with people who face a daily struggle to afford food.

stories.title: China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry Elliott
stories.summary: Free AI models that are as good as the investment-hungry US versions will disrupt global markets, and offer Britain a lesson Almost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market . Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis. Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs.
